snapshot.title: UPSC History: GoI Act 1935 & Provincial Elections
snapshot.exam_hook: 🏔️ UPSC History Hook: 1935: Autonomy/RBI/Federal Court. Center Dyarchy: 1935. 1937: Elections. 1939: Resignation. Deliverance Day: Jinnah.

quick_notes.title: GoI Act 1935: Key Features
quick_notes.detail: 1. All India Federation (never materialized). 2. Division of subjects (Federal, Provincial, Concurrent). 3. Abolished Diarchy in Provinces; Introduced Autonomy. 4. Introduced Diarchy at the Center. 5. Established RBI and Federal Court.
quick_notes.explanation: The Government of India Act of 1935 was a law passed by the British Parliament to govern India. It proposed an All India Federation, which meant a union of British Indian provinces and princely states, but this federation never actually came into existence. The Act divided government subjects into three lists: Federal subjects for the central government, Provincial subjects for the provinces, and Concurrent subjects where both could make laws. It abolished the system of diarchy, or dual government, in the provinces, where some powers were previously shared between elected ministers and British officials, and instead introduced Provincial Autonomy, giving elected provincial governments full control over their subjects. However, the Act introduced diarchy at the Centre, meaning that at the national level, some subjects like defense and foreign affairs were kept under the British Governor-General's control, while others were given to Indian ministers. Finally, the Act established the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), which is the country's central bank, and the Federal Court, which was the highest court for settling disputes between the central and provincial governments.

quick_notes.title: Provincial Elections (1937)
quick_notes.detail: INC won absolute majority in 5 provinces and formed ministries in 8 out of 11 provinces. Muslim League performed poorly.
quick_notes.explanation: Provincial Elections of 1937 refers to the elections held in British India in 1937 for the provincial legislatures, which were the law-making bodies for each province, under the Government of India Act 1935. The Indian National Congress, or INC, which was the main political party seeking independence, won an absolute majority, meaning it got more than half the total seats, in five provinces and was able to form its own government in eight out of the eleven total provinces. The Muslim League, which was a political party representing the interests of many Indian Muslims, did not perform well and won very few seats compared to the Congress. This result showed that the Congress was the most popular party among the general population, while the Muslim League's poor performance made it realize it needed to work harder to gain support from Muslims.

quick_notes.title: The 28-Month Rule
quick_notes.detail: Ministries worked on agrarian reforms, untouchability removal, and education. Proved that Indians were capable of administration. Restricted by the powers of the Governors.
quick_notes.explanation: The 28-Month Rule refers to the 28-month period from 1937 to 1939 when elected Indian ministers ran provincial governments under British rule. These ministries focused on agrarian reforms, meaning changes to land ownership and farming policies; untouchability removal, which aimed to end the social discrimination against people considered outside the caste system; and education. Their work showed that Indians were fully capable of governing themselves. However, the ministries were restricted by the powers of the Governors, who were British-appointed heads of each province and could veto laws or take over administration. This experiment ended when all Congress ministries resigned in 1939 to protest India being dragged into World War II without

quick_notes.title: Resignation of Ministries (1939)
quick_notes.detail: INC resigned because the British Government involved India in World War II without consulting the Indian people or the ministries.
quick_notes.explanation: In 1939, the Indian National Congress (INC) was the main political party leading the freedom struggle and had formed elected governments in several provinces of British India under the Government of India Act of 1935. When World War II broke out, the British government unilaterally declared India a belligerent without consulting the Indian people or the elected provincial ministries. The INC viewed this as a complete disregard for democratic consent and a violation of their rights. In protest, the Congress ordered all its provincial ministries to resign immediately. This coordinated resignation of ministries is known as the Resignation of Ministries of 1939.

quick_notes.title: Day of Deliverance
quick_notes.detail: Muslim League (under Jinnah) celebrated the INC resignation as "Day of Deliverance" on Dec 22, 1939.
quick_notes.explanation: The Day of Deliverance was an event organized by the Muslim League, a political party that aimed to protect the rights of Muslims in British India, under the leadership of Muhammad Ali Jinnah. It was celebrated on December 22, 1939, to mark the resignation of the Indian National Congress (INC), the major party fighting for Indian independence, from all provincial governments. The INC resigned because the British government had declared India a participant in World War II without consulting Indian leaders. Jinnah and the Muslim League argued that this resignation freed Muslims from what they saw as Congress's oppressive rule, so they called it a "Day of Deliverance" and held public meetings to thank God. The event deepened the political divide between the INC and the Muslim League, pushing India closer to the eventual partition in 1947.

topic_title: UPSC History: GoI Act 1935 & Provincial Elections
lesson_intro: Today we study the 'Blueprint of the Indian Constitution'. The Government of India Act 1935 was the longest act passed by the British Parliament and is the single largest source for our current Constitution. We also study the 28-month rule of the INC in provinces (1937-39). For UPSC, focus on 'Provisional Autonomy', 'Diarchy at the Center', and 'Why the INC resigned in 1939'. This is the structural transition to self-rule.
